audit-trail-verify-it-yourself.title: Anchor a receipt signed with your own Stellar key
audit-trail-verify-it-yourself.excerpt: Hash it, sign it with a Stellar key, POST it, and get a CID that anyone can check. Free during the beta.
audit-trail-verify-it-yourself.h1: Anchor a receipt signed with your own Stellar key
audit-trail-verify-it-yourself.p1: An agent acts. An agent pays. Later, someone asks who did what, and when. If the only answer lives in your own database, you are asking people to trust you.
audit-trail-verify-it-yourself.p2: Audit Trail gives you another answer. You anchor a fingerprint of the evidence to IPFS and sign it with a Stellar key. Anyone can check it without asking us.
audit-trail-verify-it-yourself.step1_p: Take the bytes you want to be able to prove later and compute their sha-256. The evidence itself stays with you.
audit-trail-verify-it-yourself.step2_p: Sign the exact text nirium-audit-v1:<sha-256> with your Stellar key. A Stellar G address is an ed25519 public key, so any Stellar key pair works. The prefix stops a signature made for something else from being reused here.
audit-trail-verify-it-yourself.step3_p: Send the hash and the signature to POST /api/audit/log. The box checks the signature. If it is wrong, it answers 400 and anchors nothing. If it is right, it pins a small document to IPFS and returns its CID.

audit-trail-verify-it-yourself.example_p2: Then the request, exactly as it was sent:
audit-trail-verify-it-yourself.example_p3: The box answered 201 with a CID:
audit-trail-verify-it-yourself.example_p4: The document it pinned is public. This is what the CID returns:
audit-trail-verify-it-yourself.example_p5: We also sent a request signed by a different key than the one it claimed. The box answered 400, with an error that names the exact text to sign, and anchored nothing.
audit-trail-verify-it-yourself.evidence_doc_label: The anchored document from this run
audit-trail-verify-it-yourself.verify_p1: You do not need to trust the box. You need the CID and your original evidence. This script downloads the document, recomputes the sha-256, rebuilds the signed text and checks the ed25519 signature against the G key.
audit-trail-verify-it-yourself.verify_p2: This is the output of the real run, with the right evidence:
audit-trail-verify-it-yourself.verify_p3: We also changed one word of the evidence, from approved to rejected. The hash check printed false and the script exited with an error. Run it with your own CID and your own evidence.
audit-trail-verify-it-yourself.h_limits: What it proves and what it does not
audit-trail-verify-it-yourself.limit1_p: The document has not changed since it was pinned, because its CID comes from its content. The hash matches your evidence. The holder of the G key signed that hash.
audit-trail-verify-it-yourself.limit2_p: It does not prove that the content is true. It does not say who is behind a G key in real life. The anchoredAt field is the time the box wrote into the document, not an independent timestamp.
audit-trail-verify-it-yourself.limit3_p: IPFS records cannot be deleted. Anchor the hash of your evidence. The optional record field is capped at 8KB, and you are responsible for what you put in it.
audit-trail-verify-it-yourself.limit4_p: Free during the beta and rate-limited. The box sets the network, not the request: it anchors on whichever network it runs on, mainnet or testnet, never the one the client asks for.
audit-trail-verify-it-yourself.mainnet_p1: We ran the exact flow above against the mainnet box too, with a separate throwaway key and this evidence: {"action":"approved","ref":"demo-receipt-mainnet-001"}. It anchored the same way: 201, a CID, a document that verifies.

audit-trail-verify-it-yourself.close_p1: Run the two scripts with a key of your own. Start with GET /api/audit/info, which lists the current rules.
audit-trail-verify-it-yourself.where_body: GET /api/audit/info lists the rules, the limits and the two endpoints. POST /api/audit/log anchors a hash.

bbva-open-deal-room.title: Nirium at The Open Deal Room by Stellar — BBVA Tower, Mexico City
bbva-open-deal-room.excerpt: We were one of six Stellar startups featured at La Arena inside BBVA Tower CDMX. Here is what we showed, who was in the room, and why an autonomous treasury agent belongs in front of institutional investors.
bbva-open-deal-room.h1: Nirium at The Open Deal Room by Stellar
bbva-open-deal-room.p1: On May 21, 2026, Nirium was featured at The Open Deal Room by Stellar, hosted inside BBVA Tower in Mexico City. We were one of six Stellar ecosystem startups invited to La Arena — a curated room where builders present in front of venture investors, angels, and institutional players active in the Mexican fintech landscape.
bbva-open-deal-room.p2: It is not every day that an autonomous, on-chain treasury agent gets to stand in the lobby of one of Latin America's largest banks. That contrast is exactly the point.
bbva-open-deal-room.pitch_hook_quote: As a founder, I was my own treasurer — and I slept. So did the money.
bbva-open-deal-room.pitch_problem: We opened with a problem every Mexican founder feels: corporate cash sits idle. It loses roughly 10% a year to inflation while it sleeps in an account, and keeping it productive is a 24/7 manual job nobody has time for.
bbva-open-deal-room.pitch_solution: Then the turn — Nirium wakes the money that sleeps. An autonomous agent moves idle USDC into CETES, Mexican sovereign debt, through Etherfuse, and back to liquid the moment it is needed: instantly, and without a treasury desk.
bbva-open-deal-room.pitch_team: We closed on the team: Giovanny Amador (Founder) and Monserrat Mendoza (Co-founder) — the same duo that placed 3rd at the Fintech World Cup México with a previous project. A team that has already shipped and won together.
bbva-open-deal-room.presented_p1: We walked the room through the core of Nirium: a non-custodial agent that moves idle corporate USDC into Mexican government bonds (CETES) through Etherfuse, 24/7, with a Soroban contract enforcing every transfer.
bbva-open-deal-room.presented_p2: The message we kept returning to is the security pattern that makes this safe to put in front of institutions. An AI agent can read the market and propose a rebalance, but it never holds custody — a 2-of-3 Soroban multisig vault enforces delegation scopes on-chain, so a compromised or hallucinating agent physically cannot move funds the contract did not authorize.
bbva-open-deal-room.pattern_quote: The LLM proposes, the contract decides.
bbva-open-deal-room.venue_p1: Tokenized real-world assets in Mexico are no longer a thesis on a slide. CETES on Stellar via a regulated operator is a live corridor, and seeing it discussed inside BBVA Tower — rather than a hackathon side room — signals how quickly institutional appetite is forming. Nirium's position is deliberately software-only and non-custodial: regulated partners handle settlement, while we provide the rails developers and fintechs embed.
bbva-open-deal-room.takeaway_p1: Beyond the pitch, the value of La Arena was the conversations it opened — with investors and ecosystem operators who understand both the Stellar stack and the Mexican regulatory context. Those are the relationships that turn a working testnet protocol into a funded, audited, mainnet product. We left with new threads to pull, and a clearer read on what institutional partners need to see next: verifiable adoption, not promises.
bbva-open-deal-room.where_body: Nirium runs an autonomous agent on Stellar testnet and published TypeScript and Python SDKs. On mainnet, x402 payments, Audit Trail and Reporting already run, receive-only and non-custodial; MPP is experimental. NiriumVault, our own treasury contract, remains audit-gated. Backed by the Stellar ecosystem: two-time Stellar Community Fund Instawards recipient (via the Stellar Ambassador Program) and an active Stellar Mexico Ambassador.

treasury-node-verify-it-yourself.title: The Treasury Node on Mainnet: Don't Trust Us, Verify the Contract
treasury-node-verify-it-yourself.excerpt: Nirium's agent holds the RebalanceManager role on a real DeFindex vault on Stellar mainnet — and the vault's own contract code makes withdrawal structurally impossible for that role, not just against our policy. Here is the transaction, the exact line of source code that proves it, and what it means for everyone involved.
treasury-node-verify-it-yourself.h1: The Treasury Node on Mainnet: Don't Trust Us, Verify the Contract
treasury-node-verify-it-yourself.p1: Most "non-custodial" claims in this industry are a policy: a team says it won't move your funds, and you decide whether to believe them. Ours is a constraint enforced by a smart contract we don't control. This post walks through one real transaction that proves it, and what that proof is worth to everyone standing near it — DeFindex, Etherfuse, OtterSec, the Stellar ecosystem, the people who'd eventually trust an agent with real money, and Nirium itself.
treasury-node-verify-it-yourself.p2: Nothing here is a summary you have to take on faith. Every hash, contract address, and line of code below is a link — go check it.
treasury-node-verify-it-yourself.fact_p1: On August 6, 2026 at 00:56:39 UTC, an address controlled by Nirium's agent called `rebalance()` on a live DeFindex vault on Stellar mainnet, with an `Invest` instruction, moving 1.0 CETES from the vault's idle balance into DeFindex's Etherfuse strategy. No human clicked anything. Transaction:
treasury-node-verify-it-yourself.fact_p2: The address that signed this specific transaction has since rotated to a new key — routine operational hygiene, not a scandal. The vault's current RebalanceManager is itself a public, on-chain fact, readable by anyone by calling the vault's own `get_rebalance_manager()` view function — nothing about who holds this role is hidden behind our word.
treasury-node-verify-it-yourself.fact_p3: Here's the part that actually matters: this isn't a policy Nirium chose to follow. It's what the vault contract's own code allows the RebalanceManager role to do, full stop. `rebalance()` accepts exactly two instructions that move value — `Unwind` and `Invest` — and neither takes a destination address as an argument. `Unwind` hardcodes the destination to `e.current_contract_address()`, the vault itself; `Invest` has no destination parameter at all, funds only ever move into a strategy the vault already trusts. Withdrawing to an arbitrary address isn't blocked by a check somewhere — there's no code path that accepts one. Every other real capability — pausing a strategy, rescuing funds, changing which address holds a role — belongs to the Manager, a role Nirium's agent does not hold.
treasury-node-verify-it-yourself.evidence_strategy_label: The Etherfuse strategy it invested into
treasury-node-verify-it-yourself.evidence_source_label: The exact source code — rebalance(), Unwind and Invest
treasury-node-verify-it-yourself.evidence_roles_label: DeFindex's own docs on vault roles
treasury-node-verify-it-yourself.evidence_audit_label: OtterSec's audit of this vault contract family
treasury-node-verify-it-yourself.h_why: Why this matters, beyond this one transaction
treasury-node-verify-it-yourself.why_p1: "We don't custody your funds" is the most common sentence in DeFi, and by itself it's worth nothing — it's exactly what a team about to run off with your money would also say. What changes the calculus isn't the sentence, it's whether the claim is checkable by someone with no reason to trust you. A contract's source code is checkable. A team's intentions are not.
treasury-node-verify-it-yourself.why_p2: That's the actual shift this transaction demonstrates: from "trust us" to "here's the code, here's the transaction, go verify both yourself." Nirium doesn't hold the role that could take custody even if we wanted to — DeFindex's Manager role does, and on this vault, that role belongs to the vault's owner, not to us. The agent proposes and executes rebalancing; it structurally cannot walk away with the money.
treasury-node-verify-it-yourself.h_impact: What this means, actor by actor
treasury-node-verify-it-yourself.impact_intro: This isn't one story — it's a different, specific claim for each party near it, and none of them are ours to make unilaterally. Here's what each one can actually check.
treasury-node-verify-it-yourself.impact_defindex_p: A vault architecture is only as strong as its worst integration. This is a real third party — not DeFindex's own documentation, not a synthetic test — putting real value through the RebalanceManager role exactly as designed, on mainnet, with the outcome publicly verifiable. That's a harder validation than any internal test suite can produce, and it's evidence DeFindex can point to, not just claim.
treasury-node-verify-it-yourself.impact_etherfuse_p:
CETES on Stellar just gained one more real, automated, and now-verified path into it — capital moving into the Etherfuse Blend strategy without a human at a terminal, and without anyone having to trust the party operating that automation. That's a concrete answer to the question every potential integrator asks before connecting to a yield product: what happens if the thing sending me capital gets compromised? Here: nothing it isn't allowed to do, because the contract won't let it.

And it's not just technical traction: Etherfuse already operates on two real legal foundations, not a promise — a no-action relief from Mexico's CNBV (Resolution P090/2024, April 16, 2024, granted to Etherfuse Liquid) and its Stablebonds registered as ledger-based securities under Swiss law (Art. 973d of the Code of Obligations). This automated flow adds to that foundation; it doesn't depend on it.
treasury-node-verify-it-yourself.impact_ottersec_p: An audit report proves code was reviewed. A real transaction, months later, behaving exactly the way that audited code says it should, proves the review held up outside a lab — under a real integration nobody wrote specifically to pass a test. That's a stronger claim than "audited": audited and confirmed in production.
treasury-node-verify-it-yourself.impact_stellar_p: Non-custodial DeFi automation is a common pitch and a rare mainnet artifact. This is one concrete, dated, on-chain example of an autonomous agent moving real value between DeFi primitives on Stellar without ever holding custody of it — not a roadmap slide, not a testnet demo, a transaction anyone can decode themselves.
treasury-node-verify-it-yourself.impact_clients_h: For the people who'd eventually trust an agent with real money
treasury-node-verify-it-yourself.impact_clients_p: To be direct about where this stands today: the vault in this post is Nirium's own team proving the mechanism with its own funds, not an outside client's money yet — worth saying plainly, since the whole point of this post is not overstating what's verifiable. What it gives a future client isn't a promise that it'll work when it's their turn. It's something to check before they ever have to take our word for anything: the exact contract, the exact role, the exact transaction, all public, all today.
treasury-node-verify-it-yourself.impact_nirium_p: This is the kind of evidence that doesn't inflate under scrutiny — it's stronger the harder someone looks at it, which is the opposite of most claims made in this space. For the Stellar Community Fund and for any future partner evaluating whether the non-custodial claim is real, this transaction and the three lines of contract code behind it are the actual differentiator, not a line in a pitch deck.
treasury-node-verify-it-yourself.regulatory_map_p: One more thing, for completeness: converting USDC to CETES in this flow touches three separate regulatory regimes, not one — Circle (USDC's issuer) holds a full MiCA license in the EU and multiple licenses in the US, but no direct Banxico/CNBV authorization to operate in Mexico; Etherfuse operates under its own Mexican no-action relief and Swiss registration, also without being a licensed Mexican bank. Neither is doing anything improper — this is simply the real map of who regulates what, without flattening it.
treasury-node-verify-it-yourself.close_p1: Every link above resolves to something you don't have to take our word for — a live block explorer, a public GitHub repository, a documentation page DeFindex controls, not us. Decode the transaction. Read the contract. If something here doesn't hold up the way this post says it does, that's worth knowing — for you and for us.
treasury-node-verify-it-yourself.where_body: Nirium's Treasury Node runs on mainnet as the RebalanceManager on DeFindex vaults the client owns — invite-only during legal review of a specific open question under Mexico's anti-money-laundering law (LFPIORPI, Art. 24 Bis 4) on virtual-asset intermediation, with a public, client-signed path (propose-and-sign) available to anyone today. x402 and audit anchoring are live on both testnet and mainnet; MPP is testnet-only.

x402-outage-verify-it-yourself.title: Mainnet x402 Was Down for 32 Days: Don't Trust Us, Verify the Fix
x402-outage-verify-it-yourself.excerpt: Every paid mainnet request against Nirium's x402 endpoints failed for 32 days — not from our code, but from a stale RPC URL inside a facilitator we don't operate. Here's the root cause, the two independent real payments that prove it's fixed, and the permanent logging hook we shipped so the next one doesn't take a month to notice.
x402-outage-verify-it-yourself.h1: Mainnet x402 Was Down for 32 Days: Don't Trust Us, Verify the Fix
x402-outage-verify-it-yourself.p1: Every payment product built on a standard it doesn't fully control eventually meets the same test: what happens when the thing you depend on breaks, and it isn't your code? For 32 days, mainnet x402 payments against Nirium's endpoints failed on every attempt — not from a bug we wrote, but from a misconfiguration inside a facilitator we don't operate and can't patch ourselves. This post is the arc end to end: what broke, how we proved it wasn't ours, how it got fixed, and what we shipped so the next outage doesn't need an outside report to be noticed.
x402-outage-verify-it-yourself.p2: Nothing here is a summary you have to take on faith. Every transaction hash, GitHub comment, and file below is a link — go check it.
x402-outage-verify-it-yourself.fact_p1: Starting around August 10, 2026, every mainnet x402 settlement against Nirium's paid endpoints — and against every other integrator using the same hosted facilitator — began failing with `unexpected_verify_error`, a catch-all for an unhandled exception inside the facilitator's own `verify()` call. Not a rejected payment: the facilitator never got far enough to evaluate one. Isolation testing that day, and every day after, showed the same pattern: the identical client and payload settled cleanly on testnet, and failed the same way on mainnet, every single time.
x402-outage-verify-it-yourself.fact_p2: We filed OpenZeppelin/relayer-plugin-x402-facilitator#47 on August 19. Three independent integrators — us, AgentLedger, and a third party — converged on the exact same finding across a month of silence on two official OpenZeppelin channels. What actually broke it open wasn't the thread or a support-forum post: it was tagging, by handle and directly, the two maintainers we'd verified were still active elsewhere in the org. One replied within a day.
x402-outage-verify-it-yourself.fact_p3: The root cause, once posted: the hosted pubnet facilitator instance was pointed at a stale RPC URL, so `verify()` threw before it ever reached the payload. We retested the same afternoon with a real settlement against our own mainnet endpoint — clean `200`, confirmed on Horizon. A second, fully independent team ran the identical test the next day, with the same result. Two teams, two payments, two different days, one root cause:
x402-outage-verify-it-yourself.evidence_issue_label: The issue we filed — now closed
x402-outage-verify-it-yourself.evidence_devlog_label: Our own devlog entry, dates and all
x402-outage-verify-it-yourself.h_why: Why this matters, beyond this one outage
x402-outage-verify-it-yourself.why_p1: Every payment product built on x402 — ours included — depends on a facilitator it doesn't operate. That dependency is real, not theoretical, and pretending otherwise doesn't make an outage less likely. What actually changes the outcome is whether the failure gets found, diagnosed with the same discipline as a bug in your own code, and made visible instead of quietly retried into invisibility.
x402-outage-verify-it-yourself.why_p2: The right response to depending on infrastructure you don't control isn't to hide when it breaks — it's to instrument it, diagnose it with method, and leave permanent visibility behind so the next failure doesn't need an outside report to be noticed.
x402-outage-verify-it-yourself.h_impact: What this means, actor by actor
x402-outage-verify-it-yourself.impact_intro: This isn't one story — it's a different, specific claim for each party near it. Here's what each one can actually check.
x402-outage-verify-it-yourself.impact_openzeppelin_p: A hosted facilitator carries real operational weight — every integrator's paid traffic routes through it, and a silent misconfiguration on their side is invisible from ours until someone reports it from outside. Once tagged directly, the actual fix (correcting the pubnet RPC URL) landed within two days, and it's held under two independent teams' real settlements since. That outcome matters more than how long the silence lasted.
x402-outage-verify-it-yourself.impact_fernando_p: His own mainnet payment hit this exact outage on September 4, blocked by something entirely outside his control or ours. He stayed in the thread, retried the day after the fix shipped, and posted his own independent confirmation — a second real settlement, a different account, the same clean result. That's stronger evidence than any single team re-testing its own fix.
x402-outage-verify-it-yourself.impact_stellar_p: This ran entirely on mainnet, against real infrastructure, with real fee-sponsored USDC settlements — not a testnet demo standing in for one. A facilitator outage affecting a whole ecosystem is exactly the kind of failure that's easy to describe in the abstract and hard to prove was real; this post exists so nobody has to take that part on faith either.
x402-outage-verify-it-yourself.impact_clients_p: The mainnet paid path is reliable again, confirmed by two separate teams on two separate days — not just our own word that it's fixed. Nothing changes on the integration side: the same client, the same endpoints, the same header. If it failed for you during this window, it wasn't your integration.
x402-outage-verify-it-yourself.impact_nirium_p: We shipped a server-side logging hook mid-outage — `onAfterVerify`/`onVerifyFailure` on the facilitator client, writing every rejection reason and payer address into our own logs instead of only being visible from outside. It stays in place permanently, not as a workaround for this specific bug: it's the difference between finding the next facilitator regression ourselves and waiting for another integrator to report it first.
x402-outage-verify-it-yourself.close_p1: Every link above resolves to something you don't have to take our word for — a live block explorer, a GitHub issue thread, our own devlog entry with the dates and root cause spelled out. Decode the transactions. Read the thread. If something here doesn't hold up the way this post says it does, that's worth knowing — for you and for us.
x402-outage-verify-it-yourself.where_body: x402 runs live on both testnet and mainnet today — the same endpoints, the same client, the same header, nothing changed by this incident except that a facilitator-side failure now lands in our own logs the moment it happens instead of after someone else notices first. Update, 2026-10-04 (checked against the nirium 0.16.0 changelog that day): this paragraph originally said MPP Charge also runs live on mainnet. That was wrong: MPP Charge is experimental and not available on mainnet.
